name: Leg shaving

lead: Leg shaving is the removal of leg hair at skin level. Wikipedia notes that bodybuilders and male models shave so muscles look more defined, and that it has long been standard in cycling and swimming; women's leg shaving became common in the West in the early 20th century as hemlines rose.[1]

The appearance payoff is a smooth, uniform surface on which muscle shape, tone and tan or oil show more clearly, which is why physique competitors and many gym-goers do it. Shaving is described as the least expensive and one of the least painful removal methods.[1]

paras: People use a razor or an electric shaver, often with shaving cream or gel; alternatives include waxing, sugaring, depilatories, epilators and lasers.[1] Because shaving cuts hair at the surface, stubble reappears within days, so people repeat it on a schedule that suits them, often before photos, competitions or events.

Shaving can cause razor burn, nicks and ingrown hairs. Case reports describe folliculitis after leg shaving, including molluscum contagiosum spread to shaved skin and a Muay Thai fighter with Dermatophilus congolensis folliculitis after frequent shaving and close contact in training.[3][2] Clean blades and skin care are the usual advice in dermatology literature.

lead: Leg shaving is the removal of hair from the legs with a razor or electric shaver. It is common among women for aesthetic reasons and, among men, mainly in sport and physique culture.[1]

Wikipedia reports that cyclists and swimmers began shaving around the turn of the 20th century, swimmers for reduced drag, cyclists for easier wound cleaning and massage, and that bodybuilders and male models shave to make muscles look more defined.[1] More men now shave for appearance alone.[1]
Published literature on leg shaving is mostly dermatology case reports about complications such as folliculitis rather than trials of cosmetic effect.[2][3]
infobox: Razor, electric shaver; alternatives include waxing, sugaring, lasers[1]

paras: Shaving cuts hair at or just below the skin surface. Wikipedia describes it as the least expensive and one of the least painful ways to remove leg hair, with waxing, sugaring, depilatory creams, epilators and laser as alternatives.[1] Women often use razors designed for the legs rather than face razors.[1]

Wikipedia notes that women's leg shaving became common in Western countries from the early 20th century, around the First World War, as hemlines rose and swimsuits became more revealing. Men's shaving in sport dates to around the turn of the 20th century.[1] The Roman writer Seneca is cited as seeing leg hair removal as a mark of effeminacy.[1]

Among athletes, listed reasons include reduced drag in swimming, easier cleaning of road rash in cycling, and less pain from tape pulling and therapeutic massage.[1] In physique sports, shaving makes muscle definition more visible.[1]

Dermatology literature includes a case of molluscum folliculitis after leg shaving[3] and a 2026 case report of recurrent folliculitis from Dermatophilus congolensis in a contact-sport athlete who shaved frequently and trained in humid conditions; authors suggested transmission through contact and shared mats.[2]

No studies found on cosmetic effects of leg shaving. Related published work consists of case reports of shaving-associated folliculitis[2][3] and a study teaching leg shaving to women with disabilities using video prompting.[4]
